A RRIF payment can arrive as securities: keep the bank-cash plan beside it

Four interactive graphics separate a hypothetical gross RRIF payment, securities received outside the plan, actual bank cash and the cash assigned to tax and household bills.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 5 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Original hypothetical same-date CAD ledger, assuming a carrier-approved ordinary minimum-payment illustration and a separate non-registered destination for securities. No source deductions, fees, sale, price change, settlement delay or return is modeled. All values use the same assumed transfer-date valuation. The selected gross payment is capped at entered available RRIF value; any unrepresented request is reported separately and is not a finding of a statutory breach. The calculator does not determine the legal minimum, issuer availability, tax liability, contribution room, benefit effects or cost basis. Income-tax cash is an independently entered earmark, not a tax calculation. Both tax and household spending are budget assignments; the displayed bank balance is measured before either is paid. A negative budget remainder is an unfunded assignment, not a negative bank account or automatic loan.

The central idea

A payment recorded outside a RRIF is not necessarily a deposit of spendable cash. Confirm its form and keep unsold securities separate from the money assigned to the next bill.

01

Ask what actually arrives when the RRIF makes a payment

A retirement statement can show a payment without the same number of dollars reaching the bank. The distinction matters when a household has assigned that payment to rent, groceries or an income-tax bill.

Paragraph 5 of the CRA’s IC78-18R7 Registered Retirement Income Funds explains that the minimum amount may be paid in a form other than cash. The carrier and the account arrangement still need to confirm what can be delivered and how the actual payment will be valued and recorded.

An in-kind payment moves property, such as securities, outside the RRIF without automatically selling it for cash. The illustration assumes an approved ordinary minimum-payment arrangement and a separate non-registered destination. It does not calculate the minimum or decide whether a particular account supports that form.

This is distinct from transferring assets directly between registered arrangements. The example follows a payment to the annuitant. CRA’s RRIF overview states that amounts paid out are taxable on receipt; a payment’s non-cash form does not make this illustration a tax-free withdrawal.

02

Split the gross amount before putting it in the cash budget

The worked example begins with a RRIF value of CAD 400,000 immediately before the illustrated payment. The independently entered carrier-confirmed gross payment is CAD 25,000. The model does not derive that amount from the current balance or an age factor.

At a 60% securities share, CAD 15,000 arrives as securities and CAD 10,000 arrives as bank cash. The RRIF value falls by CAD 25,000 to CAD 375,000, holding prices unchanged. The two payment components total the same CAD 25,000; they are not two withdrawals of that size.

The household also has CAD 12,000 of opening bank cash. After the cash component arrives, its bank balance is CAD 22,000 before the tax and spending assignments are paid. The CAD 15,000 of securities remains a separate asset.

With no fees, withholding, market movement or completed household payments in this example, the resources reconcile. Opening RRIF value plus bank cash is CAD 412,000. The later RRIF value of CAD 375,000, securities of CAD 15,000 and bank cash of CAD 22,000 add to the same total. Movement between locations has not created wealth.

03

An earmark changes availability before it changes the bank balance

The selected tax cash reserve is CAD 6,000, and planned household bills total CAD 18,000. Together they assign CAD 24,000 of cash. Against the CAD 22,000 bank balance, the illustration has an additional cash requirement of CAD 2,000.

The waterfall is a budget-capacity bridge. Its negative endpoint does not mean the actual bank account is already overdrawn. Neither assignment is treated as a completed payment. It shows that the same bank balance cannot fund both promises in full.

The tax amount is entered independently after a separate assessment. It is not a percentage calculated by this tool or a statement of final tax owing. The illustration assumes no tax is withheld from the payment; if actual source deductions or fees apply, replace this simplified cash plan with the carrier’s real net receipts and the remaining tax requirement.

Unsold securities are excluded from bank cash. Selling them could change the plan, but would require a separate decision, price, transaction cost, tax review and receipt date. The calculator supplies no automatic sale or borrowing facility to fill the shortage.

04

Test the form while keeping the total payment unchanged

The line varies the securities share while keeping the gross payment and both cash assignments fixed. At an all-cash mix, the CAD 25,000 payment adds to CAD 12,000 opening cash. After assigning CAD 24,000, the budget has CAD 13,000 left.

At an all-securities mix, no new bank cash arrives. Opening cash alone leaves CAD 12,000 of the two assignments unfunded. Both mixes represent the same CAD 25,000 payment in this illustration, but they create very different cash capacity.

The selected defaults reach a zero budget remainder at a 52% securities share: the remaining 48% supplies CAD 12,000 of cash. That crossing is conditional arithmetic. It does not recommend a payment mix or establish which securities should remain invested.

The matrix also changes opening bank cash. More accessible cash can fund a larger securities share without an immediate shortage. A zero cell answers only whether these two entered assignments can be funded now; it does not prove that future expenses, taxes or retirement needs are covered.

05

Confirm the payment record and the usable cash separately

For an actual arrangement, confirm the remaining payment requirement, the available form, the valuation used, the destination account and the expected delivery dates with the carrier. Then prepare a separate budget using the cash actually expected to reach the bank and the tax amount still to be funded.

The model caps the represented payment at the available RRIF value and identifies any unrepresented selected amount. That is a limit of the cash illustration, not a ruling that a statutory minimum has been breached. Changes in account value and special circumstances belong with the carrier’s actual calculation.

Keep the withdrawal record, the securities position and the bank statement in distinct roles. One documents the payment, one shows property still held, and one supplies money available for cash obligations. Reconciling all three prevents a gross retirement payment from being spent twice in the plan.
